questions.stem: An unshielded point source produces 18 mrem per hour at 2 feet. Approximately what dose rate is expected at 6 feet?
options: 6 mrem per hour
2 mrem per hour
9 mrem per hour
54 mrem per hour
incorrectOptionExplanations: This assumes dose rate changes directly with distance.
This divides by two rather than by the square of the distance ratio.
This multiplies the dose as distance increases.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 28, distance and inverse-square control, pp. 642-646; NRC protection principles

questions.stem: A sealed source begins at 160 MBq and passes through three half-lives. What activity remains?
options: 40 MBq
80 MBq
20 MBq
120 MBq
incorrectOptionExplanations: Forty MBq remains after two half-lives, not three.
Eighty MBq remains after one half-life.
This subtracts a fixed amount rather than halving each period.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 28, radioactive decay and half-life, pp. 640-642

questions.stem: A maintenance task near a gamma source cannot be eliminated. Which plan best applies radiation protection principles?
options: Rely only on cotton gloves
Increase time near the source to complete work slowly
Remove shielding to improve visibility
Reduce time, maximize practical distance, use suitable shielding, and monitor dose
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Time, distance, shielding, containment, planning, and dosimetry are combined to keep exposure controlled and as low as reasonably achievable.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Gloves do not provide effective shielding from penetrating gamma radiation.
Dose generally increases with exposure time.
Removing shielding increases dose rate unless another analysis justifies the change.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 28, radiation-control methods, pp. 642-648; NRC protection principles

questions.stem: Why can an alpha-emitting powder be a serious hazard despite low external penetration?
options: Internal deposition after inhalation or ingestion can deliver high localized energy
Alpha particles pass easily through thick steel
Alpha radiation is nonionizing
The material becomes harmless when airborne
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Skin can stop most external alpha particles, but contamination control is critical because internalized emitters irradiate tissue directly.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Alpha particles have short range and poor external penetration.
Alpha radiation is ionizing.
Airborne dispersion can increase the chance of internal intake.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 28, alpha radiation and biological effects, pp. 636-640

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes radiation exposure from radioactive contamination?
options: Exposure always means radioactive material is inside the body
Exposure is irradiation; contamination is unwanted radioactive material on or in a person or area
Contamination ends immediately when the source is turned off
The two terms have exactly the same meaning
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Exposure describes interaction with radiation, while contamination involves radioactive material that can be transferred or internalized.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A person can be exposed to an external source without becoming contaminated.
Contamination may remain after an external source is removed or a device is de-energized.
The distinction affects monitoring, decontamination, and control.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 28, radiation basics and control methods, pp. 636-648

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a personal dosimeter for a radiation worker?
options: Provide shielding for the entire body
Remove radioactive contamination from clothing
Measure and document the worker cumulative external dose
Identify every radionuclide in a sample
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Personal dosimetry supports dose monitoring, investigation, work planning, and compliance with exposure-control programs.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A dosimeter records dose; it is not a body shield.
Decontamination requires removal or cleaning methods.
Radionuclide identification requires appropriate survey or analytical instrumentation.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 28, radiation control and monitoring, pp. 642-648; NRC radiation protection

questions.stem: Which shielding choice is generally most appropriate for penetrating gamma radiation?
options: A thin sheet of paper
Only a cotton garment
An open air gap with no distance increase
Dense material such as lead or substantial concrete, selected by energy and required attenuation
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Shield type and thickness depend on radiation type and energy; dense materials are commonly used for gamma attenuation.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Paper can stop alpha particles but provides little gamma attenuation.
Ordinary clothing does not adequately attenuate penetrating gamma photons.
An air gap helps only if it increases distance; it is not shielding by itself.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 28, shielding, pp. 645-648; NRC protection principles

questions.stem: A high-power laser beam crosses an occupied walkway. Which control is strongest?
options: Enclose or terminate the beam path and interlock access where feasible
Post a sign and leave the beam open
Require workers to look away while passing
Use laser eyewear as the only control
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Engineering controls that contain the beam and prevent access are stronger than reliance only on warnings and PPE.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A warning does not prevent direct or reflected beam exposure.
Behavior alone is unreliable around an invisible or unexpected beam path.
Eyewear is important but should not replace enclosure, beam stops, and access control.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 28, lasers and laser safety-control measures, pp. 652-654
